notes.meaning: Boaz went to the town gate, which was the public meeting place and open-air court in ancient Israel. He watched for the closer relative to walk by and invited him over to sit down. God guided the timing so the man arrived right when Boaz was ready to settle the matter.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read Ruth as a kind of fairy tale. In their view, "Mr. So-and-so" is a playful nonsense name, and Boaz beats him with clever words.

notes.meaning: Boaz gathered ten leaders of the town to sit with them as an official council. While two or three witnesses were enough for simple matters, ten made up a legal court for weighty decisions like land sales and marriage. Their presence guaranteed that the agreement would be completely binding.

Boaz explained that Naomi had returned from Moab in poverty and needed to sell the family land that had belonged to Elimelech. Under God's law, family land was not to be lost forever, so a close relative was expected to buy it back. Boaz mentioned Naomi first to lay out the property situation clearly before bringing up the topic of marriage.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think Naomi was not selling the land itself. They think she was giving up her right to buy it back and use it, perhaps in return for support.

notes.meaning: Boaz told the man that he had the first legal right to redeem the land in front of the town leaders. Boaz also made it clear that if the man did not buy it back, Boaz was next in line to do so. The relative agreed at once, thinking it was a simple chance to expand his own estate.

Boaz then explained the second part of the responsibility that came with the purchase. Buying the land also required marrying Ruth the widow, so that any son born to her would carry on Mahlon's family name and inherit that field. Boaz connected the duty of buying the land with caring for the family line.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that Hebrew manuscripts vary between reading 'you acquire' and 'I acquire,' and they question whether this was a strict levirate marriage since Boaz and the relative were not Mahlon's brothers.

notes.meaning: When the man learned that marrying Ruth was part of the deal, he backed out and gave up his right to Boaz. He worried that spending his money on the field and raising an heir for another man would hurt his own children's inheritance. He cared more about protecting his personal wealth than helping his needy relatives.

In ancient Israel, handing over a sandal was an old custom used to confirm a property transfer, showing that a man gave up his right to step on the land as owner. Because the relative politely stepped aside rather than defying a direct command, he gave up his shoe without the public shame usually shown to an unwilling brother. By handing over his sandal, he legally transferred all his redemption rights to Boaz.

Boaz called on the elders and all the people at the gate to witness the transaction. He announced that he was buying from Naomi everything that had belonged to Elimelech and his two sons, Mahlon and Chilion. This open statement settled the purchase before the whole town.

Boaz also announced that he was taking Ruth the Moabitess to be his wife. His goal was to keep the name of Mahlon alive on his family property so it would not disappear from Bethlehem. Because Ruth had turned from idols to trust the Lord, her marriage into Israel was honorable.

The leaders and the townsfolk confirmed they were witnesses and gave a joyful wedding blessing. They prayed that the Lord would make Ruth as fruitful as Rachel and Leah, the two mothers who built up the nation of Israel. They also asked that Boaz would prosper and be honored throughout Bethlehem.

The people prayed that Boaz's family would grow to be like the house of Perez, the son born to Judah and Tamar. Perez was the founding ancestor of the Bethlehem clan to which Boaz belonged. The community recognized that every true blessing of children comes directly from the Lord.

Boaz took Ruth home as his wife, and the Lord blessed her with conception so that she gave birth to a son. Scripture highlights that the gift of new life comes entirely from God's gracious hand. Ruth, once a childless foreign widow, was now an honored mother in Israel.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the book was written partly to push back against the later ban on foreign wives in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah.

notes.meaning: The women of Bethlehem praised the Lord alongside Naomi for providing a family redeemer to care for her. Although Boaz carried out the legal redemption, the women pointed to the newborn baby as the one who secured her family's future. God turned Naomi's bitter grief into deep thanksgiving.

The women told Naomi that the child would restore her joy and provide for her in her old age. They praised Ruth, saying that her selfless love made her more valuable to Naomi than seven sons. True love within God's family brings blessings far greater than anyone expected.

Naomi tenderly took her new grandson onto her lap and became his loving caregiver. Holding the baby showed that she embraced him as the heir of her departed family. Her past days of emptiness were completely healed by God's kindness.

The neighborhood women celebrated the baby as a son born to Naomi and named him Obed, which means 'servant' or 'one who helps.' The name showed the comfort and care he would provide to his grandmother in her later years. Obed grew up to become the father of Jesse, who was the father of King David.

The family record traces the line of Judah from Perez through Hezron, Ram, and Amminadab to Nahshon. Nahshon served as the chief leader of the tribe of Judah during Israel's time in the wilderness, and he became the father of Salmon. This list shows how God preserved and guided generations of faithful family history.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point out that Ruth is left out of this all-male list. They argue she is still the true hero of the book.

notes.meaning: The family line continues from Salmon to Boaz, from Boaz to Obed, from Obed to Jesse, and finally to David. This record reveals that the book of Ruth is not just a personal family story, but part of God's larger plan to bring forth Israel's greatest king. God used the faithfulness of ordinary people to prepare the royal line that would lead to Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point out that Ruth is left out of this all-male list. They argue she is still the true hero of the book.
